opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think modality matters a lot more than people appreciated in the early days of the algorithmic fairness literature. If you go back ten years or so, almost all of the theoretical and even empirical work implicitly assumed tabular data. You had a lending dataset or a criminal justice dataset, there was a column for race or gender, and you had a well-defined prediction task: will this person repay the loan, will they recidivate. In that setting, you can write down fairness definitions pretty crisply. Equalize false positive rates across groups, or equalize approval rates, and then you can study the tradeoffs between accuracy and those constraints, and design algorithms that navigate that Pareto frontier.

When you move to modalities like images, speech, or especially free-form text from generative models, a lot of that crispness goes away. First, the group attributes often aren't explicitly present. There's no column that says what the demographic of a person in a photo is, and trying to infer it raises its own set of ethical and technical problems. Second, and maybe more fundamentally, the notion of what a "decision" or an "error" is becomes much fuzzier. If a language model writes a story or answers an open-ended question, what does it mean for that output to be fair? It's not a binary classification where you can count false positives by group.

So my view is that the core concepts carry over. You still want to think about which groups you're worried about, what harms you're trying to prevent, and how to measure disparities. But the operationalization has to be rethought for each modality. With speech recognition, you might look at word error rates across dialects or accents, which is fairly measurable. With image generation, you might worry about representational harms, like whether prompts for "a doctor" produce a narrow demographic slice. With text generation, it gets very contextual and you often need human judgment or carefully designed evaluation sets.

One thing I'd emphasize, from my time thinking about this both in academia and in industry, is that the science of measurement has become the bottleneck. In the tabular world, measurement was the easy part and the algorithms were the interesting research. In these richer modalities, it's almost flipped. If you can't reliably measure a fairness property, you can't optimize for it, you can't audit for it, and you can't make credible claims about it. So I think a lot of the important responsible AI work now is in developing rigorous, scalable evaluation methodologies that are tailored to the modality, rather than just porting over definitions that were designed for credit scoring.

r001.rationale: The response says early fairness research implicitly assumed tabular data with a column for race or gender, and contrasts this with modalities where group attributes are not explicitly present.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, Sam, great to be here. I think modality matters a lot more than people tend to acknowledge in fairness work, and I'll say up front that it's a point where I've had to update my own thinking.

When Aaron Roth and I were writing The Ethical Algorithm, and in most of the research my group was doing at the time, we were implicitly living in a tabular world. You've got rows, you've got columns, and one of those columns is race or gender or age. The protected attribute is right there in the data, it's categorical, and so the whole fairness enterprise gets framed around it. You pick your definition, demographic parity or equalized odds or whatever it is, you measure the disparity across those groups, and you build algorithms that constrain or correct it. That framing is clean and it produced a lot of good science. But the cleanliness comes largely from the modality.

Once you move to images, or audio, or free-form text, several things change at once. The first is that the sensitive attribute is no longer a column. It's latent. A photo doesn't come with a race field, but the pixels carry an enormous amount of information correlated with it, and a model will happily pick that up without anyone explicitly feeding it in. So the question of what you're even measuring fairness with respect to becomes much harder, and the old move of just dropping the protected feature becomes essentially meaningless.

The second thing is that the notion of a group gets much richer and much blurrier. In a spreadsheet you have a handful of discrete categories. In an image, or in speech, you have skin tone, lighting, accent, dialect, age, all of it continuous and intersecting. That actually connects to work we did on subgroup fairness, where the point was that protecting a few coarse groups doesn't protect the intersections. In high-dimensional modalities you're forced to confront that immediately, because there's no natural small set of groups to begin with.

And the third, which I think is underappreciated, is that the harms look different. With tabular models in lending or hiring, the harm is typically a decision that goes against you, a denial. With a speech recognizer that works worse for certain accents, or a language model that represents certain populations in a stereotyped way, the harm is about quality of service and representation. Those aren't well captured by a confusion matrix, and a lot of the mathematical fairness definitions were built on the confusion matrix.

So where I've landed is that the modality is not a detail you sort out after you've chosen a fairness definition. It largely determines which definitions are even coherent, how you'd measure them, and often whether you need to go collect additional information just to know what the groups are. The core ideas transfer, the idea that you have to be explicit about what you're trading off and that you should measure it, but the machinery has to be rebuilt, and I think the field is still fairly early in doing that for the modalities that generative models have made dominant.

r001.rationale: The response says prior fairness research implicitly assumed a tabular dataset with a race, gender, or age column, making the protected attribute directly available.

astra-6.text:
I think the data modality matters a great deal, because fairness isn’t a single property that you can define independently of the task. You have to ask what the data represents, what decision you’re making, and who could be harmed by that decision.

With tabular data, for example, you might be making lending decisions, and you can ask fairly concrete questions about approval rates or error rates across demographic groups. Those questions still involve difficult choices, but the outcomes and the groups you want to examine may be relatively easy to specify.

With images or language, there are additional questions about representation and context. Does a vision system work equally well for different populations? Does a language system associate particular groups with particular occupations or stereotypes? Those are different kinds of concerns, and reducing all of them to the same statistical test can miss what matters.

So I’d say the modality helps determine how unfairness can manifest and how you can measure it. But the application is essential, too. The same data can support very different decisions, with very different consequences. You need to understand both before choosing a fairness definition or a technical intervention.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how modality and application shape fairness concerns, but it does not say that fairness research often assumes protected-group demographic attributes are already present in the dataset.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the modality matters a great deal, because fairness isn’t a property you can define independently of what the data represents and how the model is being used. If you’re working with tabular data for a lending decision, you might have a clearly defined outcome and demographic attributes that let you ask whether error rates differ across groups. Even there, you have to decide which differences matter and what the consequences are.

With language or images, the questions can look quite different. You might be concerned about stereotyping, representation, or whether a system performs poorly for particular dialects or skin tones. Those concerns don’t necessarily reduce to the same statistical test you would use for lending.

So I’d distinguish the mathematical tools, which can sometimes carry across modalities, from the work of specifying the problem. What constitutes harm? Who is affected? What would a fairer outcome look like? The modality shapes those questions, but the application and the people affected have to shape the answers.

r001.rationale: The response mentions demographic attributes in its lending example, but does not say that fairness research often assumes protected-group attributes are already present in the dataset.
